m00.body:
## What this pack is steering

The rep's words, verbatim: *"claims ops people at mid-sized UK insurers who are drowning in complaints"*. Direct motion, 20 firms wanted, three weeks, email and LinkedIn only. The rep has since widened the region: the locked scope is **GB and IE** — Great Britain plus the Republic of Ireland — with roles narrowed to **claims operations**. That widening is the most important thing about this run. The earlier pack for this product (cmtvknbpe002dkwozlhiav3c3) was built entirely inside Great Britain; everything about the Irish market is, by definition, absent from it. This run keeps what still stands in GB and adds the firms the Republic of Ireland now makes reachable.

This is a bench run limited to the steering note and the targeting specification, so the argument below is compressed to what a targeter needs.

**The spine.** Claims and complaint handling in general insurance is a telephone process, and quality assurance on that telephony is done by human sampling — an analyst listens to a handful of calls per handler per month and fills in a form. The product's live capability is that every call the pipeline ingests is transcribed and scored against the customer's own QA rules, with configurable risk types and a per-call record holding the transcript, the per-rule breakdown, the summary and the coaching points. That is the displacement: sampled human QA out, scored-on-ingest QA in. Complaints are the wedge because a complaint is where an unreviewed call becomes a cost — an ombudsman case, an uphold, a remediation exercise, a client's oversight finding.

**Why the widening changes the argument and not just the map.** In Great Britain the urgency clock is the Financial Ombudsman Service's per-case fee and the FCA's supervisory work on claims handling and third-party oversight. Neither instrument exists in the Republic of Ireland: the Irish complaints route is the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman, the conduct rulebook is the Central Bank of Ireland's Consumer Protection Code rather than the FCA Handbook, and the supervisory vocabulary is different. A targeting recipe that carries FCA language into Dublin will read as foreign. The two countries share the underlying operational fact — claims telephony reviewed by sample — and share nothing of the regulatory furniture around it. Everything that follows is built so the GB and IE halves can be worked with the same product argument and different evidence.

One quiet advantage the widening creates: hosting is EU (Frankfurt), which in Great Britain is a thing to explain and in the Republic of Ireland is an unremarkable answer to a data-residency question. That is an inference from the hosting fact, not a finding about Irish buyers.

**Size is the filter that does the real work.** The product's own band is 5 to 250 contact-centre seats. Published headcount is not seat count, and in insurance the gap is wide: a carrier with 800 staff may run a 90-seat claims floor, and a broker with 200 staff may run none at all because claims are delegated out. In practice the band selects MGAs with delegated claims authority, third-party claims administrators, travel and assistance desks, specialist motor and niche personal-lines operations, and the central complaints functions of broker consolidators — not the composite majors, whose claims floors run into the thousands of seats. In the Republic of Ireland the band is less of a constraint and more of a description: the whole market is smaller, and a mid-tier Irish insurer's claims operation frequently sits inside the band where its British equivalent would not.

**What must not lead.** Three of the most tempting insurance angles are boundaries. There are no regulator-ready evidence packs. There is no in-app audio playback, so "listen to the evidence" is out. There is no group or cross-tenant dashboard, which bites in exactly this market because MGAs, TPAs and cross-border Irish–British groups will ask for a view across entities. There is no PII or card redaction and no SSO or SCIM; a regulated buyer's security review will ask and the honest answer is no. The product is post-call only, does not record calls, and results land within a couple of hours rather than minutes.

**Telephony is the first disqualifier, not the last.** Automated feeds exist for 3CX, OAK/ClarifyGo and RingCentral. Everything else — Teams, Cisco, Avaya, Mitel, 8x8, Five9 — is "works with recordings from", scoped per customer. Insurance estates in both countries skew to Teams, Avaya and Genesys-class platforms, so a scoping conversation should be assumed and framed as a qualifying question rather than a claim.

**What the prior pack asserted, carried here as hypotheses only.** No claim from cmtvknbpe002dkwozlhiav3c3 enters this pack without a fresh page found this run. Its four situations — the outsourced claims handler, the travel and assistance claims desk, the delegated-authority MGA and the specialist motor claims operation — are treated as a hypothesis about the shape of the market, re-tested here, and its eleven seed firms are treated as candidates to be re-sourced rather than as findings.
m00.spine: Claims telephony in general insurance is reviewed by human sample — a few calls per handler per month — so the conversations that turn into complaints are almost always conversations nobody reviewed. Scoring every ingested call against the operation's own QA rules turns that blind spot into a queryable record, at a price with no seat minimum, which is what puts it inside reach of a claims operation of 5 to 250 seats in Great Britain or the Republic of Ireland.

hypotheses: Prior pack hypothesis, to re-test: the four buying situations are the outsourced claims handler, the travel and assistance claims desk, the delegated-authority MGA and the specialist motor claims operation. Treated here as a shape to test against fresh pages, not as a finding.
Prior pack hypothesis: a per-case ombudsman fee is a sharper trigger for a claims operations buyer than a conduct-rulebook obligation, because it has a number and a date attached.
Prior pack hypothesis: claims-handling TPAs feel the pain harder than carriers, because they are judged on a client's complaint numbers and must produce evidence about calls the client cannot see.

Prior pack hypothesis, and the one the widening most threatens: that roughly half of regulated contact centres already report reviewing every call with AI, so coverage alone is not a surprising opener. Whether that holds in the Republic of Ireland is unknown and must not be assumed from British research.

New hypothesis created by the widening: the Republic of Ireland's smaller market means a mid-tier Irish carrier's claims operation falls inside the 5 to 250 seat band where its British equivalent would not, so the same seat filter selects larger-brand firms in IE than in GB.
New hypothesis: Irish buyers will treat EU (Frankfurt) hosting as unremarkable where British buyers treat it as a question to answer, making the data-residency conversation cheaper in IE.

Prior pack seed firms are candidates only. The eleven firms it held (Claims Consortium Group, S&G Response, AllClear, Healix International, Collinson, Hood Group, Commercial Express, Slick Cover, Sabre Insurance Group, Marshmallow, Aioi Nissay Dowa UK) enter this pack only if re-sourced with a fresh dated page this run.

m00.displacement: Manual sampled QA: a QA analyst listening to four to eight calls per handler per month and completing a scoring form, supported by a spreadsheet and a monthly report. The incumbent is a person and a process, not a rival product — and in outbound the contrast is always drawn against that status quo, never against a named vendor.

m04.body:
## How to find these operations, and how to throw most of them away

The hard part of this brief was never finding insurance firms in Great Britain and the Republic of Ireland. It is finding the ones whose claims telephone operation sits inside 5 to 250 seats, and then finding the ones where that operation is actually theirs. Two filters do almost all the work, and both of them bite harder now that the scope covers two countries.

**Filter one: who actually answers the phone.** The single most useful thing this run found is that in travel and home insurance the brand on the policy is frequently not the operation on the call. AllClear's own contact page names Gallagher Bassett as its claims handler; Voyager Insurance's claims page names Gallagher Bassett too; three separate Irish travel brands — multitrip.com, InsureandGo Ireland and annualtravelinsurance.com — all route claims to MAWDY Travel Claims in Galway. A lead-gen recipe built on insurance brand names will therefore spend most of its budget writing to firms whose claims conversations are somebody else's. The practical instruction is mechanical and cheap: before a firm goes on the list, open its claims page and read whose telephone number is on it. That page is public, it is free, and it settles the question in thirty seconds.

The same rule works in reverse, and this is the discovery route for the operations that never appear in any register of insurers: the claims pages of a dozen brands will name the same handful of handlers, and those handlers are the buyers with the seats.

**Filter two: headcount is not seats, and it cuts both ways.** Three firms that looked like obvious seeds were dropped on size or on filter one. Claims Consortium Group's own trade-body entry puts it at 330 people across multiple sites; Hood Group's public profile puts it at 201 to 500; AllClear states 400-plus employees and outsources the claims desk anyway. None of them is disqualified as a business — they are disqualified as seeds for a 5-to-250-seat product where the buyer's own telephone operation has to fit the band and nobody has published a seat count. Where a firm states its own team size plainly, as S&G Response, Sabre and KennCo do, it is worth more than any database estimate, and every seed below carries the honest status of what is known.

**What changed with the Republic of Ireland, and what did not.** The product argument is identical on both sides of the Irish Sea; the evidence around it is not. In Great Britain the dated instruments are the Financial Ombudsman's case fee and the FCA's published review work — and the FCA's review of 15 home and 8 travel insurers is unusually well aimed at this campaign, because the areas for improvement it names are limited control over outsourced claims arrangements and poor management information, which is precisely the gap a sampled QA process leaves. In the Republic there is no case fee and no FCA Handbook: the instruments are the Central Bank's modernised Consumer Protection Code, in force since 24 March 2026, and the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman. A recipe that carries FCA vocabulary into Dublin or Galway will read as imported. Use the Irish sources for Irish firms.

One structural observation, offered as an inference rather than a finding: the Irish market's smaller scale means the seat filter selects differently there. A new Irish motor entrant that has publicly committed to a 300-person workforce is, today, a contact centre inside the band and, within a year, possibly outside it — which makes the Irish half of this list time-sensitive in a way the British half is not.

**On triggers.** The strongest signals in this market remain dated regulatory and financial events — a published review, a trading update, a rebrand or a new authorisation — rather than hiring noise. Claims-handler job adverts run continuously in both countries and prove nothing on their own; they are listed below as WARM and only ever as corroboration. Where a seed's signal is thin, it is labelled thin rather than dressed up: the S&G Response signal is the firm's own dated commentary on TPA growth, not a contract win, and no contract win was found this run.

**Seed firms are a validation sample, not the list.** Ten firms are named below so a rep can check by hand whether these recipes produce the right shape of company. Three are in the Republic of Ireland and would not have been reachable under the earlier brief; none is reused across two kinds of buyer; and no single list page supplied more than one of them.

claims.text: The FCA reviewed the claims handling arrangements of 15 home insurance providers and 8 travel insurance providers, and among the areas for improvement it names 'lack of control over outsourced arrangements' and 'poor management information'; among good practice it names well-established claims governance using consistent and robust MI and multi-faceted oversight of outsourced activities, such as regular quality assurance checks and customer journey testing.

The FCA states its concerns about the impact of service failings are more pronounced for travel insurance claims, because those claims are often made in emergency circumstances and are characterised by time sensitivity, logistical complexity and increased customer vulnerability.

From 1 April 2026 respondent financial businesses have a case fee allowance worth GBP 2,000 for the financial year, after which the maximum case fee is GBP 680 per case, payable regardless of the outcome of the complaint.

The FCA's firm-specific complaints data set is composed of submissions from approximately 290 individual firms reporting either 500 or more complaints within a six-month period or 1,000 or more annually; firms below those thresholds appear only in the aggregate statistics, and the current data set was published on 15 May 2026.

The Central Bank of Ireland's modernised Consumer Protection Code took effect on 24 March 2026 after a twelve-month implementation period, and the Central Bank marked its coming into force on that date.

Several Irish travel insurance brands direct policyholders to the same outsourced claims desk: annualtravelinsurance.com Ireland and multitrip.com both tell customers to contact MAWDY Travel Claims on an 091 (Galway) number and to post claim forms to 22-26 Prospect Hill, Galway, and InsureandGo Ireland gives an 091 claims number with a mawdy.com email address.

In Great Britain the same pattern appears: AllClear tells customers that its claims handler is Gallagher Bassett, and Voyager Insurance states that all Voyager Plus claims are handled by Gallagher Bassett.
claims.inferredFrom: provenance: fewer than two of its distinctive words on the page (appears, bassett, pattern)

claims.text: Three otherwise plausible firms sit above the product's seat band on published headcount or outsource the claims desk: Claims Consortium Group's trade-body entry states 330 people across multiple sites, Hood Group's public company profile states 201-500 employees, and AllClear states 400-plus employees while naming an external claims handler.

The Central Bank of Ireland publishes downloadable registers including an Insurance Distribution Register and a register of non-life undertakings regulated by the Central Bank, each dated to a stated day (both listed as at early August 2026 when read).

m14.body:
## What changed, and why it is not the same pack with two more countries stapled on

This run reads one prior pack for Insights360 (cmtvknbpe002dkwozlhiav3c3), built entirely inside Great Britain for the rep's original brief. The rep has since widened the region to Great Britain and the Republic of Ireland and narrowed the role filter to claims operations specifically. Under this org's rule, nothing from that earlier pack enters this one unless a fresh url found this run supports it — so what follows is not a diff of text, it is a re-test of every claim and every seed firm against pages read this run.

The four kinds of buyer held. The prior pack's outsourced claims handler, travel and assistance claims desk, delegated-authority MGA and specialist motor claims operation were re-tested rather than assumed, and all four survived the wider scope under the same archetype ids, now populated with a mix of British and Irish firms.

The regulatory argument did not simply transfer. The prior pack's urgency rested on the FCA Handbook and the Financial Ombudsman's case fee, neither of which reaches an Irish entity. This run found the Republic's own dated instrument — the Central Bank of Ireland's modernised Consumer Protection Code, in force since 24 March 2026 — sitting where the FCA material sat for Great Britain, and it is now load-bearing for every Irish seed firm in m04.

On seed firms: three of the prior pack's eleven are kept, each re-sourced with a fresh dated signal this run (S&G Response, Commercial Express, Sabre Insurance Group). One, AllClear, is not a simple drop — it is a correction: this run found AllClear's own contact page names Gallagher Bassett as its claims handler, contradicting the prior pack's implicit treatment of AllClear as an in-house claims desk. Two more, Claims Consortium Group and Hood Group, are dropped on a size check this run performed and the prior pack did not: both sit above the product's seat band on their own published headcount. The remaining five prior seeds — Healix International, Collinson Insurance, Slick Cover, Marshmallow and Aioi Nissay Dowa Insurance UK — are not carried forward at all: no fresh dated url for any of them was found this run, so they lapse rather than being re-asserted on last run's evidence. Seven new seed firms were added in their place, five of them reachable only because the region now includes Ireland (MAWDY Ireland, Blue Insurance, KennCo Underwriting, Pen Underwriting Ireland, OUTsurance DAC) and two found fresh in Great Britain (ClaimSorted, Just Travel Cover).

No price change was found: the facts file's per-seat plans, overage rate and setup fees are unchanged from what the prior pack cited.

Claims Consortium Group's trade-body entry states 330 people across multiple sites and Hood Group's public company profile states 201-500 employees, both above the product's stated seat band on published headcount.
S&G Response Ltd, Commercial Express Quotes Ltd and Sabre Insurance Group plc are the three prior-pack seed firms kept in this pack, each re-sourced with a fresh dated signal this run.

MAWDY Ireland, Blue Insurance, KennCo Underwriting, Pen Underwriting Ireland and OUTsurance DAC are five new seed firms in Ireland, each with its own page read this run: MAWDY's careers page, Blue Insurance's contact page, KennCo's homepage, Pen Underwriting Ireland's about-us page and OUTsurance's homepage.

Published per-seat pricing (GBP 4.99 / 7.99 / 9.99 per seat per month, GBP 0.50 per hour overage, GBP 1,280 setup and GBP 640 configuration review, no seat minimum, no annual lock-in) is unchanged from the prior pack.

changes.text: Region widened from Great Britain only to Great Britain and the Republic of Ireland, and the role filter narrowed to claims operations. The prior pack's four kinds of buyer (outsourced claims handler, travel and assistance claims desk, delegated-authority MGA, specialist motor claims operation) were re-tested rather than assumed and held under the wider scope, keeping the same archetype ids.

A dated regulatory instrument entered the pack that the Great-Britain-only prior pack could not hold: the Central Bank of Ireland's modernised Consumer Protection Code took effect on 24 March 2026, giving Irish claims operations a dated conduct obligation distinct from the FCA Handbook and the Financial Ombudsman's case-fee regime the prior pack relied on for its urgency.

Three of the prior pack's eleven seed firms are kept, each re-sourced with a fresh dated signal found this run: S&G Response Ltd (sandgresponse.co.uk), Commercial Express Quotes Ltd (commercialexpress.co.uk) and Sabre Insurance Group plc (sabreplc.co.uk).

The prior pack listed AllClear Insurance Services as a seed firm; this run found AllClear's own contact page names Gallagher Bassett as its claims handler, and separately found three Irish travel brands routing claims to a comparable outsourced desk (MAWDY). AllClear is not carried forward as a seed for the travel and assistance claims desk kind of buyer as a result.

Two of the prior pack's seed firms are dropped on a size check this run performed and the prior pack did not: Claims Consortium Group (330 people across multiple sites, per its own trade-body entry) and Hood Group (201-500 employees, per its public company profile), both above the product's seat band.

Five of the prior pack's seed firms — Healix International, Collinson Insurance, Slick Cover, Marshmallow and Aioi Nissay Dowa Insurance UK — are not carried into this pack: no fresh dated url for any of them was found this run, so under the rule that a prior claim enters only with a fresh url found this run, they lapse rather than being re-asserted.

Seven new seed firms were added. Five are reachable only because of the widening to the Republic of Ireland: MAWDY Ireland (mawdy.ie), Cover-More Blue Insurance Services / Blue Insurance (blueinsurance.ie), KennCo Underwriting (kennco.ie), Pen Underwriting Ireland (penunderwriting.ie) and OUTsurance DAC (outsurance.ie). Two are new Great Britain firms found this run: ClaimSorted (claimsorted.com) and Just Travel Cover (justtravelcover.com).
